This book covers AS topic 1 (basic economic ideas and resource allocation) — scarcity, opportunity cost, economic methodology, factors of production, economic systems, production possibility curves and the classification of goods — and the core exam skills used throughout Papers 2 and 4: data calculations, data response technique, diagrams, and writing 8-, 12- and 20-mark essays. Marks are awarded for knowledge and understanding (K), analysis (An) and evaluation (Ev); calculations use M1 (method) and A1 (answer). Every calculation was checked by computer. The mark guides are our own and are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost

Key ideas

  • The basic economic problem: wants are unlimited but resources are finite, so there is scarcity and choices must be made.
  • The three questions: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.
  • Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
  • Economic decision-makers: consumers, firms and governments all face scarcity and trade-offs.
  • Margin: many choices are about "a little more or a little less" (marginal decisions).

Worked examples

Example 1: a government spends $50 million on a new hospital instead of a new highway. The opportunity cost is the highway (the next best alternative), not "everything else".

Example 2: a student works 10 hours a week at $8 an hour instead of attending revision classes. The opportunity cost of attending classes would be $80 a week of earnings.

Example 3: a farmer with 100 hectares grows wheat rather than maize; the opportunity cost is the maize output forgone.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Define opportunity cost. [2]

(b) Explain why scarcity means every economy must answer three basic questions. [4]

(c) A student can spend 3 hours either working for $12 per hour or studying. Calculate the opportunity cost of studying and explain one reason why the student may still choose to study. [4]

Answers and mark guide:

  • (a) The value of the next best alternative (K1) given up when a choice is made (K1).
  • (b) Resources are limited relative to wants, so not everything can be produced (K1); societies must decide what to produce (An1), how to combine resources to produce it (An1) and how to distribute output among people (An1).
  • (c) 3 × $12 = $36 (M1 A1); studying may raise future earnings or exam success, which the student values more than $36 now (Ev2).

Common mistakes

  1. Defining opportunity cost as "all alternatives".
  2. Confusing scarcity with shortage.
  3. Saying rich countries have no scarcity.
  4. Forgetting non-money opportunity costs (time).
  5. Listing the three questions without linking them to scarcity.

Quick recall

  1. Define scarcity.
  2. Three basic questions?
  3. Define the margin.
  4. Does a free gift have an opportunity cost for society?
  5. Who faces scarcity?

Answers: 1) Wants exceed the resources available to satisfy them. 2) What, how, for whom. 3) A small additional change (one more or one less unit). 4) Yes — resources used to make it could have made something else. 5) Consumers, firms and governments.
